"Bu API üyesinin adını/argümanlarını sürümünüz için doğrulayamıyorum. API Help'te `IModelDoc2` altında arayın ya da makro kaydedicisiyle bir örnek kaydedip bana gönderin; ona göre uyarlayayım."

docs.title: Welding, Fasteners and Finishing for Sheet Metal
docs.text:
Welding, Fasteners and Finishing for Sheet Metal › Overview

# Welding, Fasteners and Finishing for Sheet Metal (Kaynak, Bağlantı Elemanları, Yüzey İşlemi)

docs.title: Welding, Fasteners and Finishing for Sheet Metal
docs.text:
Welding, Fasteners and Finishing for Sheet Metal › 1. Joining options

| Method | Good for | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| TIG (ISO 4063 process 141) | Thin sheet, stainless, aluminium, visible seams | Slow, skill-dependent |
| MIG/MAG (131 / 135) | Mild steel, production welding | Spatter, distortion on thin sheet |
| Resistance spot (21) | Overlapping sheets, high volume | Needs access from both sides; surface marks |
| Projection welding (23) | Weld nuts/studs | Tooling |
| Laser welding | Low distortion, thin sheet | Fit-up tolerance, equipment |
| Self-clinching fasteners (PEM-type nuts, studs, standoffs) | Threads in thin sheet, no welding | Sheet hardness and minimum thickness limits; hole size; edge distance |
| Welded studs (capacitor discharge) | Studs on thin sheet | Mark on the back side |
| Blind rivets | Fast, no heat | Visual, strength limits |
| Clinching (press joining) | No consumables | Tool access |
| Screws/bolts and nuts | Serviceable joints | Torque, loosening, gasket compression |

docs.title: Welding, Fasteners and Finishing for Sheet Metal
docs.text:
Welding, Fasteners and Finishing for Sheet Metal › 2. Welding design points

1. **Distortion** grows with heat input and joint length on thin sheet; use short stitch welds + tacks, balanced welding sequence, fixtures, and avoid long continuous seams unless sealing is required.
2. **Sealing seams** (IP enclosures) must be continuous and leak-checked; grind flat if the gasket crosses it.
3. **Galvanised steel**: the zinc coating is burnt away near welds; fumes require extraction; touch-up coating needed.
4. **Stainless**: heat tint reduces corrosion resistance; remove by pickling/passivation after welding; protect from carbon-steel contamination (separate tools).
5. **Aluminium**: oxide layer, high thermal conductivity, filler choice (e.g. 5xxx wire for 5754) — specify per welding procedure.
6. Weld symbols on drawings follow ISO 2553 (reference line, arrow line, elementary symbol, dimensions, "all around" and "field weld" signs). Without a symbol the drawing does not define the weld.
7. Weld quality levels: ISO 5817 (steel/nickel), ISO 10042 (aluminium). Acceptance criteria belong in the specification.

docs.title: Welding, Fasteners and Finishing for Sheet Metal
docs.text:
Welding, Fasteners and Finishing for Sheet Metal › 3. Self-clinching fasteners (PEM-type)

- The fastener is pressed into a punched/laser-cut hole in a **softer** sheet; the sheet flows into a groove and locks it.
- Check the manufacturer's datasheet for: **minimum sheet thickness**, **hole diameter and tolerance**, **minimum distance hole-centre to edge**, **maximum sheet hardness**, **installation force**, **push-out and torque-out values**.
- The hole for the fastener differs from the clearance hole for a screw; note it on the drawing and in the DXF.
- Do not paint or powder-coat the thread unless masked/ tapped after finishing; define it.
- Install **before** finishing only if the finish is compatible (galvanic/ hardness/ masking).

docs.title: Welding, Fasteners and Finishing for Sheet Metal
docs.text:
Welding, Fasteners and Finishing for Sheet Metal › 4. Finishing

| Finish | Typical thickness (check supplier) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Powder coat (elektrostatik toz boya) | ≈ 60–120 µm per coat, 60–80 µm common | Cures at high temperature; thickness adds to dimensions (both faces + edges); mask threads, earth points, gasket faces if required; specify RAL colour, gloss, texture, standard |
| Wet paint | 40–120 µm by system | Primer + topcoat; solvent rules |
| Electro-galvanising (elektro galvaniz) | ≈ 5–25 µm + passivation | Thin; for indoor or mild environments |
| Hot-dip galvanising (EN ISO 1461) | ≈ 45–100+ µm | For fabricated parts; thin sheet can distort; vent/drain holes needed |
| Pre-galvanised sheet (DX51D+Z) | Z-coating mass, e.g. Z100–Z275 | Cut edges and welds unprotected |
| Stainless passivation / pickling | — | Restores passive layer after welding; specify method and standard |
| Anodising (aluminium) | ≈ 5–25 µm (type II); hard anodising thicker | Colour variation between batches; dimensional growth |
| Brushed / polished (stainless, aluminium) | Grain direction | Specify grit and direction; protective film |
| Passive: oiling, protective film | — | Shipping protection |

Specify: finish type, thickness range, colour/standard, **areas to mask**, **hanging mark locations**, and acceptance criteria (adhesion, appearance).

docs.title: Welding, Fasteners and Finishing for Sheet Metal
docs.text:
Welding, Fasteners and Finishing for Sheet Metal › 5. Interaction with enclosure design

A coating on a gasket face changes flatness and compression; a coated earth-bonding point loses electrical continuity unless masked; powder coat bridges small gaps and hides weld porosity until it breaks at the edge. See `05-enclosures-ip-ik.md`.

docs.title: Welding, Fasteners and Finishing for Sheet Metal
docs.text:
Welding, Fasteners and Finishing for Sheet Metal › 6. Review checklist

Joint accessibility for the welder/tool · distortion plan · seam type (continuous/ stitch) matches function · weld symbols present · fastener datasheet values respected · finish compatible with material and with hardware · masking defined · hanging marks defined · inspection method.

docs.title: Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work
docs.text:
Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work › Overview

# Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work (Malzeme Referansı)

Values here are **typical handbook values for first-pass work**. Certified work uses the standard and the mill certificate (3.1). Densities differ slightly between sources; always state the value used.

docs.title: Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work
docs.section: 1. Density and plate weight per m²
docs.text:
Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work › 1. Density and plate weight per m²

Weight per m² of plate = `T[mm] × ρ[kg/m³] / 1000`. Plate weight = area × that value.

| Material | ρ (kg/m³) | 1 mm | 2 mm | 3 mm | 5 mm | 10 mm |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Carbon steel DC01 / S235JR | 7850 | 7.85 | 15.70 | 23.55 | 39.25 | 78.50 |
| Stainless 1.4301 (304) | 7930 | 7.93 | 15.86 | 23.79 | 39.65 | 79.30 |
| Stainless 1.4404 (316L) | 7990 | 7.99 | 15.98 | 23.97 | 39.95 | 79.90 |
| Aluminium EN AW-5754 | 2670 | 2.67 | 5.34 | 8.01 | 13.35 | 26.70 |
| Aluminium EN AW-5052 | 2680 | 2.68 | 5.36 | 8.04 | 13.40 | 26.80 |
| Aluminium EN AW-1050 | 2710 | 2.71 | 5.42 | 8.13 | 13.55 | 27.10 |
| Copper (Cu-ETP) | 8960 | 8.96 | 17.92 | 26.88 | 44.80 | 89.60 |
| Brass CuZn37 | 8440 | 8.44 | 16.88 | 25.32 | 42.20 | 84.40 |
| Titanium grade 2 | 4510 | 4.51 | 9.02 | 13.53 | 22.55 | 45.10 |

Example: 1 m × 2 m × 3 mm carbon steel = 2 m² × 23.55 kg/m² = **47.1 kg**; in stainless 304 → 47.58 kg; in EN AW-5754 → 16.02 kg.
For a finished part use the CAD mass properties and mark them *calculated*; add hardware, welds and coating separately.

docs.title: Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work
docs.text:
Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work › 2. Grade designations and approximate equivalents

| Common name | EN | Other designations (approximate, verify) |
|---|---|---|
| DKP | DC01 (EN 10130) | St12 (old DIN), SPCC (JIS) |
| HRP / black sheet | S235JR (EN 10025-2); DD11 | St37-2 (old DIN) |
| Galvanised | DX51D+Z (EN 10346) | — |
| Stainless 304 | 1.4301 (X5CrNi18-10) | AISI 304 |
| Stainless 316L | 1.4404 (X2CrNiMo17-12-2) | AISI 316L |
| Stainless 430 | 1.4016 | AISI 430 (ferritic, magnetic) |
| Aluminium 5754 | EN AW-5754 (AlMg3) | — |
| Aluminium 5052 | EN AW-5052 (AlMg2.5) | — |
| Aluminium 1050 | EN AW-1050A | — |
Equivalent does not mean identical; chemical limits, tolerances and mechanical properties differ.

docs.title: Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work
docs.section: 3. Typical mechanical and physical values (order of magnitude)
docs.text:
Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work › 3. Typical mechanical and physical values (order of magnitude)

| Property | Carbon steel | Stainless 304 | Aluminium 5xxx |
|---|---|---|---|
| Young's modulus E | ≈ 200–210 GPa | ≈ 190–200 GPa | ≈ 69–70 GPa |
| Coefficient of thermal expansion | ≈ 11–12 ×10⁻⁶ /K | ≈ 16–17 ×10⁻⁶ /K | ≈ 23–24 ×10⁻⁶ /K |
| Yield strength (annealed/typical) | DC01 ≈ ≤ 280 MPa; S235 ≥ 235 MPa | ≈ 200–300 MPa (higher after cold work) | 5754-H22 ≈ 130–190 MPa |
| Tensile strength | DC01 ≈ 270–410 MPa; S235 ≈ 360–510 MPa | ≈ 500–700 MPa | 5754-H22 ≈ 220–290 MPa |
| Magnetic | yes | austenitic: normally not (weakly after forming) | no |
Treat these as ranges; temper, thickness and standard edition change them.

docs.title: Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work
docs.text:
Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work › 4. Forming behaviour

Mild steel: forgiving, small radii OK. Stainless: work-hardens, higher bending force and springback; larger radii. Aluminium 5xxx: good formability in soft tempers; harder tempers crack on tight radii; bend across grain.

docs.title: Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work
docs.text:
Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work › 5. Corrosion and environment

Mild steel needs coating. Galvanised: edges/welds exposed. Stainless 304: indoor, mild; 316L: chlorides/marine/chemical; passivation after welding. Aluminium: oxide layer; galvanic coupling with steel/stainless in wet environments needs isolation.

docs.title: Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work
docs.text:
Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work › 6. Weight calculation checklist

Use the **blank** area for material purchase and the **finished** mass for shipping. Confirm: grade, density used, thickness (nominal vs measured), cut-outs subtracted, coating thickness, hardware. State the formula and units: `m = V·ρ` with V in m³ and ρ in kg/m³.

docs.title: Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work
docs.section: 7. What the AI must not do
docs.text:
Materials Reference for Sheet-Metal Work › 7. What the AI must not do

Give a precise strength or equivalence without naming the standard and condition · treat 5052 and 5754 as the same · assume stainless density = steel density in a quote · invent a certificate number.

docs.title: Design Troubleshooting and Decision Support
docs.text:
Design Troubleshooting and Decision Support › Overview

# Design Troubleshooting and Decision Support

This file defines how the assistant should help when the user is **stuck**, not only when a formula is requested.

docs.title: Design Troubleshooting and Decision Support
docs.section: 1. Start from the failure mode, not the CAD command

docs.title: Design Troubleshooting and Decision Support
docs.text:
Design Troubleshooting and Decision Support › 2. Five-layer diagnosis

1. **Requirement:** what must the part do and what is non-negotiable?
2. **Geometry:** dimensions, interfaces, envelopes, clearances, datums.
3. **Material/process:** thickness, grade, bend/weld/laser/coating constraints.
4. **Assembly/service:** sequence, tool access, replaceability, cable/airflow access.
5. **Verification:** how will the requirement be measured or tested?

Do not jump from symptom to one “best” design. Generate 2–4 viable alternatives when the trade-off is real.

docs.title: Design Troubleshooting and Decision Support
Design Troubleshooting and Decision Support
Design Troubleshooting and Decision Support
docs.section: 5. “I don’t know what to ask” intake
docs.text:
Design Troubleshooting and Decision Support › 5. “I don’t know what to ask” intake

If the user only provides a screenshot or rough idea, recover the task with at most three high-value questions: intended function/environment, key dimensions/material/process, and what outcome is currently failing. Then continue with a provisional analysis rather than blocking the conversation.

docs.title: Design Troubleshooting and Decision Support
docs.text:
Design Troubleshooting and Decision Support › 6. Decision rule

Prefer a design that satisfies the stated requirement with the **fewest hidden process assumptions**. If two concepts are both viable, explain the trade-off instead of declaring a winner without the user’s priorities.

docs.title: Tolerance Stack, Fits and Functional Clearances
docs.text:
Tolerance Stack, Fits and Functional Clearances › Overview

# Tolerance Stack, Fits and Functional Clearances

docs.title: Tolerance Stack, Fits and Functional Clearances
docs.text:
Tolerance Stack, Fits and Functional Clearances › 1. Separate three questions

- **Nominal geometry:** what is the intended size/location?
- **Allowed variation:** what tolerance is assigned and under which standard?
- **Functional result:** what clearance/interference/misalignment may occur at assembly?

A drawing can be dimensionally “within tolerance” and still fail function if the datum scheme or stack path is wrong.

docs.title: Tolerance Stack, Fits and Functional Clearances
docs.text:
Tolerance Stack, Fits and Functional Clearances › 2. 1-D worst-case stack

For a signed chain `R = ±A ±B ...`, use the same signs for nominals and calculate worst-case bounds from each contributor’s limits. The helper in `tools/calculators/tolerance.py` is appropriate only when the stack is genuinely one-dimensional.

docs.title: Tolerance Stack, Fits and Functional Clearances
docs.text:
Tolerance Stack, Fits and Functional Clearances › 3. RSS/statistical stack

RSS is **not** a magic tighter tolerance. Use it only if the statistical assumptions are justified by process data and the tolerances have been converted to compatible statistical quantities. Otherwise use worst-case or a process-capability model agreed with quality/manufacturing.

docs.title: Tolerance Stack, Fits and Functional Clearances
Tolerance Stack, Fits and Functional Clearances
docs.text:
Tolerance Stack, Fits and Functional Clearances › 5. Datum selection

Datums should represent the functional locating interfaces and a realistic inspection setup. Do not choose a thin free edge as a primary datum simply because it is convenient on the drawing.

docs.title: Tolerance Stack, Fits and Functional Clearances
docs.text:
Tolerance Stack, Fits and Functional Clearances › 6. General tolerances

If a drawing references a general-tolerance standard, verify the **edition and scope**. The source registry notes that ISO 2768-1:1989 remained published while a replacement edition was under publication in 2026. Do not silently assume an old company title-block note is still current.

docs.title: Tolerance Stack, Fits and Functional Clearances
docs.text:
Tolerance Stack, Fits and Functional Clearances › 7. Output expected from the AI

A useful tolerance answer includes the stack path, signs, nominal result, worst-case result, any statistical assumption, the functional requirement being protected, and a recommendation for which dimensions should be controlled directly.

docs.title: Enclosure Thermal Management
docs.text:
Enclosure Thermal Management › Overview

# Enclosure Thermal Management

Thermal design and IP design interact. A fan opening can solve temperature and simultaneously create an ingress path.

docs.title: Enclosure Thermal Management
Enclosure Thermal Management
docs.text:
Enclosure Thermal Management › 2. First-pass forced-air calculation

For sensible heat only:
`Vdot = P / (rho × cp × ΔT)`.
`tools/calculators/thermal.py` returns m³/h after unit conversion. It is a sizing **screen**, not a fan selection: filters, grilles, pressure drop, recirculation, altitude and fan curve must then be checked.

docs.title: Enclosure Thermal Management
docs.text:
Enclosure Thermal Management › 3. Passive cooling

Do not infer passive capacity from surface area alone without a heat-transfer model and installation conditions. Natural convection, radiation, wall mounting, solar load and internal hotspots matter.

docs.title: Enclosure Thermal Management
Enclosure Thermal Management
docs.text:
Enclosure Thermal Management › 5. Deliverable

Return heat-load table, thermal assumptions, first-pass calculation, proposed architecture, ingress impact, component-selection inputs and test/measurement plan.

docs.title: Manufacturing Process Selection and DFMA
docs.text:
Manufacturing Process Selection and DFMA › Overview

# Manufacturing Process Selection and DFMA

docs.title: Manufacturing Process Selection and DFMA
docs.section: 1. Do not optimize a part before knowing volume
docs.text:
Manufacturing Process Selection and DFMA › 1. Do not optimize a part before knowing volume

Prototype, 20-piece batch and 20,000-piece production can justify different tooling and joining strategies. Always capture quantity, repeat demand and acceptable setup cost.

docs.title: Manufacturing Process Selection and DFMA
docs.text:
Manufacturing Process Selection and DFMA › 2. Process routing questions

For every feature ask:
- which operation creates it?
- does the feature survive the next operation?
- does it need a secondary setup?
- can it be inspected after forming/welding/coating?
- is there tool access and fixture access?
- does it create a special tool, manual rework or hidden setup cost?

docs.title: Manufacturing Process Selection and DFMA
docs.text:
Manufacturing Process Selection and DFMA › 3. Sheet-metal route

Typical route may include laser/turret → deburr → form → weld/insert hardware → grind/clean → finish → assemble → inspect. The actual route is supplier-specific; use it to identify risk and cost, not as a fixed universal sequence.

docs.title: Manufacturing Process Selection and DFMA
Manufacturing Process Selection and DFMA
docs.text:
Manufacturing Process Selection and DFMA › 5. Supplier capability profile

Maintain a project profile containing available material sizes, laser limits, tooling, preferred inside radii, bend table/K data, press-brake envelope, welding capability, finishes, insertion hardware and inspection tools. These project values override generic heuristics.

docs.title: Image to CAD Geometry Reconstruction
docs.text:
Image to CAD Geometry Reconstruction › Overview

# Image → CAD Geometry Reconstruction

The repository includes an executable engine under `engines/image_to_cad/`. Its purpose is **draft reconstruction**, not dimensional certification.

docs.title: Image to CAD Geometry Reconstruction
Image to CAD Geometry Reconstruction
Image to CAD Geometry Reconstruction
docs.text:
Image to CAD Geometry Reconstruction › Uncertainty

Calibration error, pixel selection, perspective, lens distortion and edge ambiguity all contribute. If the result is image-derived, use `ESTIMATED` until checked against authoritative dimensions.

docs.title: Image to CAD Geometry Reconstruction
docs.text:
Image to CAD Geometry Reconstruction › Native CAD

A DXF created from detected geometry is not equivalent to a parametric SolidWorks model. Preserve the JSON model so a future SolidWorks adapter can reconstruct constraints/features while retaining provenance.

docs.title: Image to CAD Geometry Reconstruction
docs.text:
Image to CAD Geometry Reconstruction › Release gate

No image-derived dimension should become a manufacturing dimension merely because it looks plausible. Require a drawing, measurement, supplier model, or explicit user validation for release-critical geometry.

docs.title: Requirements, Risk and Engineering Release
docs.text:
Requirements, Risk and Engineering Release › Overview

# Requirements, Risk and Engineering Release

docs.title: Requirements, Risk and Engineering Release
docs.text:
Requirements, Risk and Engineering Release › 1. Requirement record

A useful requirement is identifiable, testable and tied to a source. Record: ID, statement, source/customer, priority, verification method, status and affected parts.

Bad: “make it strong.”  Better: “door shall not permanently deform under the project-defined service load; verify by agreed test/analysis.” The actual load must come from the project, not the AI.

docs.title: Requirements, Risk and Engineering Release
Requirements, Risk and Engineering Release
docs.text:
Requirements, Risk and Engineering Release › 3. Assumption register

Every `ASSUMED`, `ESTIMATED` or `UNKNOWN` release-relevant item goes into an assumption register. Each row needs an owner and a closure action. “AI said so” is not closure evidence.

docs.title: Requirements, Risk and Engineering Release
Requirements, Risk and Engineering Release
docs.text:
Requirements, Risk and Engineering Release › 5. Change control

When a design changes, identify affected CAD, drawings, DXF, BOM, cost, quotation, test plan and documentation. A revision is not complete when only the `.SLDPRT` changed.

docs.title: Structural Stiffness and Load Paths for Sheet-Metal Designs
docs.text:
Structural Stiffness and Load Paths for Sheet-Metal Designs › Overview

# Structural Stiffness and Load Paths for Sheet-Metal Designs

docs.title: Structural Stiffness and Load Paths for Sheet-Metal Designs
docs.text:
Structural Stiffness and Load Paths for Sheet-Metal Designs › Start with function, not thickness

When a panel feels weak, first identify **what must not move and under which load**. Increasing thickness is only one option. Returns, beads, ribs, hat sections, shorter unsupported spans, different supports and better load paths can add stiffness with less mass.

docs.title: Structural Stiffness and Load Paths for Sheet-Metal Designs
docs.text:
Structural Stiffness and Load Paths for Sheet-Metal Designs › Load-path checklist

Trace the force from where it enters the design to where it reacts. For a cabinet this may be: door equipment → inner panel/stiffener → hinge → frame → shell/base → anchor/floor. A strong local feature does not help if the next interface is flexible.

docs.title: Structural Stiffness and Load Paths for Sheet-Metal Designs
docs.text:
Structural Stiffness and Load Paths for Sheet-Metal Designs › Questions before calculation

- Load magnitude/direction and whether static, impact, cyclic or transport-related.
- Support/boundary condition.
- Span and section geometry.
- Material and actual temper/grade.
- Deflection limit and permanent-deformation criterion.
- Connections: spot weld, seam weld, screw, rivet, clinch, adhesive.
- Whether the sheet behaves like a beam, plate or shell.

docs.title: Structural Stiffness and Load Paths for Sheet-Metal Designs
docs.text:
Structural Stiffness and Load Paths for Sheet-Metal Designs › Practical stiffness levers

1. Add depth to the section before adding thickness where packaging allows.
2. Put returns/stiffeners along the load path, not decoratively.
3. Break large unsupported panels into smaller effective spans.
4. Avoid abrupt stiffness transitions that concentrate load.
5. Keep stiffeners manufacturable: bend sequence, weld access, coating and drainage still matter.

docs.title: Structural Stiffness and Load Paths for Sheet-Metal Designs
docs.text:
Structural Stiffness and Load Paths for Sheet-Metal Designs › Calculation discipline

Simple beam equations are useful only for beam-like members with known boundary conditions. Broad cabinet faces are plates/shells; use an appropriate plate calculation, FEA or physical test when deformation matters. Do not report a beam idealization as exact panel behavior.

docs.title: Structural Stiffness and Load Paths for Sheet-Metal Designs
docs.text:
Structural Stiffness and Load Paths for Sheet-Metal Designs › Release evidence

Record the load case, model assumptions, inputs, result, acceptance criterion and verification method. An FEA screenshot without boundary conditions and material definition is not a release record.

docs.title: Joints, Fasteners, Hinges and Hardware
docs.text:
Joints, Fasteners, Hinges and Hardware › Overview

# Joints, Fasteners, Hinges and Hardware

docs.title: Joints, Fasteners, Hinges and Hardware
docs.text:
Joints, Fasteners, Hinges and Hardware › Choose a joint by function

A joint may locate, clamp, carry shear/tension, transmit torque, seal, conduct/bond, allow service or permanently join. State which functions matter before choosing screws, PEM hardware, rivets, welds or adhesives.

docs.title: Joints, Fasteners, Hinges and Hardware
docs.text:
Joints, Fasteners, Hinges and Hardware › Selection questions

- Permanent or serviceable?
- One-sided access or two-sided access?
- Parent sheet thickness and material?
- Static, cyclic, vibration or impact load?
- Corrosion/galvanic environment?
- Is electrical bonding required?
- Appearance constraints?
- Installation equipment available?
- How many assembly cycles?

docs.title: Joints, Fasteners, Hinges and Hardware
docs.text:
Joints, Fasteners, Hinges and Hardware › Sheet-metal hardware checks

For self-clinching or rivet hardware, use the **manufacturer's current datasheet** for minimum sheet thickness, hole preparation, edge distance, installation force and material compatibility. Do not generalize values between families.

docs.title: Joints, Fasteners, Hinges and Hardware
docs.text:
Joints, Fasteners, Hinges and Hardware › Hinges and latches

Treat hinges and latches as part of the structural and sealing system. Check door center of gravity, opening angle, interference, sag, fastener load path, service removal, latch compression distribution and gasket reaction. More latches may improve compression distribution but also increase cost and user effort.

docs.title: Joints, Fasteners, Hinges and Hardware
docs.text:
Joints, Fasteners, Hinges and Hardware › Welded vs mechanical joint trade-offs

Welding can reduce part count but introduces heat distortion, finishing effort and repair difficulty. Mechanical fastening improves serviceability but adds holes, hardware, assembly time and possible ingress paths. Compare the complete system rather than unit hardware cost.

docs.title: Joints, Fasteners, Hinges and Hardware
docs.text:
Joints, Fasteners, Hinges and Hardware › Verification

Use manufacturer ratings and project load cases. For unfamiliar hardware, prototype pull-out/torque/service-cycle behavior in the actual sheet stack before release.

docs.title: Sealing, Gaskets and Ingress-Control Details
docs.text:
Sealing, Gaskets and Ingress-Control Details › Overview

# Sealing, Gaskets and Ingress-Control Details

docs.title: Sealing, Gaskets and Ingress-Control Details
docs.section: A gasket is a system, not a strip
docs.text:
Sealing, Gaskets and Ingress-Control Details › A gasket is a system, not a strip

Ingress performance depends on the entire boundary: gasket profile, compression, door/frame stiffness, corners, seams, hardware, openings, cable entries, vents, coating and assembly variation.

docs.title: Sealing, Gaskets and Ingress-Control Details
docs.text:
Sealing, Gaskets and Ingress-Control Details › Design sequence

1. Mark one closed sealing boundary.
2. List every penetration and seam crossing it.
3. Obtain the gasket supplier's compression recommendation and environmental limits.
4. Make the compression land geometrically continuous.
5. Ensure hinges/latches distribute compression rather than creating local peaks.
6. Check tolerances and door flatness against the available compression window.
7. Check drainage separately; sealing and water management are related but not identical.
8. Prototype, inspect and test.

docs.title: Sealing, Gaskets and Ingress-Control Details
docs.text:
Sealing, Gaskets and Ingress-Control Details › Common problems

- Gasket bridges a sharp corner and lifts locally.
- Weld or seam creates a bump under the gasket.
- Powder coat changes the compression stack.
- Door is too flexible between latch points.
- A vent, gland or removable plate bypasses the intended seal path.
- Compression set reduces long-term recovery.

docs.title: Sealing, Gaskets and Ingress-Control Details
docs.text:
Sealing, Gaskets and Ingress-Control Details › IP language

Geometry can be reviewed **against an IP target**, but an enclosure is not declared compliant only from CAD. The applicable ingress tests and product conformity process determine the supported claim.

docs.title: Corrosion, Surface Finishing and Material Compatibility
docs.text:
Corrosion, Surface Finishing and Material Compatibility › Overview

# Corrosion, Surface Finishing and Material Compatibility

docs.title: Corrosion, Surface Finishing and Material Compatibility
docs.text:
Corrosion, Surface Finishing and Material Compatibility › Environment first

Indoor dry, outdoor rain, coastal salt, chemical washdown, condensation and buried/contact environments create different risks. Do not choose a coating by appearance alone.

docs.title: Corrosion, Surface Finishing and Material Compatibility
docs.text:
Corrosion, Surface Finishing and Material Compatibility › Design-for-finish checklist

- Drain/vent closed cavities where the process requires it.
- Avoid inaccessible crevices and water traps.
- Include coating buildup in tight fits, threads and gasket stacks.
- Define masking where electrical bonding or precision fits require bare metal.
- Check edge coverage and cut-edge condition.
- Ensure weld spatter/grind condition matches finish quality.
- Separate dissimilar metals when the environment and area ratio create galvanic risk.

docs.title: Corrosion, Surface Finishing and Material Compatibility
docs.text:
Corrosion, Surface Finishing and Material Compatibility › Powder coating

Specify the base material, pretreatment expectations, colour/texture, appearance class if relevant, masking and critical post-coat dimensions. A nominal coating thickness should come from the approved process/supplier specification rather than AI memory.

docs.title: Corrosion, Surface Finishing and Material Compatibility
docs.text:
Corrosion, Surface Finishing and Material Compatibility › Stainless and aluminium

Do not treat all stainless or aluminium grades as interchangeable. Fabrication route, chloride exposure, surface contamination, welding and cleaning can dominate performance.

docs.title: Corrosion, Surface Finishing and Material Compatibility
docs.text:
Corrosion, Surface Finishing and Material Compatibility › Release record

Record finish system and approved supplier/process reference, not only a colour name. Confirm how repaired welds/cut edges and field modifications will be protected.

docs.title: Metrology, Inspection and Quality Planning
docs.text:
Metrology, Inspection and Quality Planning › Overview

# Metrology, Inspection and Quality Planning

docs.title: Metrology, Inspection and Quality Planning
docs.section: Design dimensions that can be verified
docs.text:
Metrology, Inspection and Quality Planning › Design dimensions that can be verified

A dimension or GD&T control is only useful if manufacturing and inspection can establish the referenced features/datums. Avoid creating an elegant drawing that requires an unavailable measurement setup for every part.

docs.title: Metrology, Inspection and Quality Planning
Metrology, Inspection and Quality Planning
docs.text:
Metrology, Inspection and Quality Planning › Measurement planning

For each critical item state: nominal/tolerance, datum setup, tool or method, access/orientation, frequency or sampling rule, recording requirement and reaction plan. Match measurement uncertainty/capability to the tolerance being judged.

docs.title: Metrology, Inspection and Quality Planning
docs.text:
Metrology, Inspection and Quality Planning › Sheet-metal realities

Formed parts relax when unclamped; flexible panels can be distorted by the fixture. Define whether inspection is free-state, restrained or assembled when this changes the result. Measure hole patterns and interfaces from functional datums rather than accumulating chained dimensions where possible.

docs.title: Metrology, Inspection and Quality Planning
docs.text:
Metrology, Inspection and Quality Planning › First article / prototype

Use early builds to validate both the part and the measurement method. A repeated disagreement between CAD and inspection can be a datum/fixture problem, not only a fabrication problem.

BOM, Revision, PDM and Engineering Change Control › Overview

# BOM, Revision, PDM and Engineering Change Control

docs.title: BOM, Revision, PDM and Engineering Change Control
docs.text:
BOM, Revision, PDM and Engineering Change Control › One change affects many artifacts

Changing a hole, thickness or finish can affect part CAD, assembly, drawing, DXF, STEP, BOM, mass, cost, quotation, work instruction, inspection plan and stock. Release is a synchronized set, not one saved CAD file.

docs.title: BOM, Revision, PDM and Engineering Change Control
docs.text:
BOM, Revision, PDM and Engineering Change Control › Minimum item identity

Each manufactured/bought item should have a stable part number or identifier, description, revision/state, quantity/unit and make/buy classification. Avoid using filenames as the only identity system.

docs.title: BOM, Revision, PDM and Engineering Change Control
docs.text:
BOM, Revision, PDM and Engineering Change Control › Revision discipline

Distinguish work-in-progress from released data. Record why a revision changed and what downstream artifacts were regenerated. Do not silently overwrite an issued DXF or PDF with a new geometry under the same released identifier.

docs.title: BOM, Revision, PDM and Engineering Change Control
docs.text:
BOM, Revision, PDM and Engineering Change Control › PDM-safe automation

Macros/scripts that rename or move referenced SolidWorks files can break assemblies when used outside the approved PDM/rename workflow. Prefer reporting and controlled exports over bulk destructive changes.

docs.title: BOM, Revision, PDM and Engineering Change Control
docs.text:
BOM, Revision, PDM and Engineering Change Control › ECO/ECN checklist

Problem/reason → affected items → proposed change → technical review → cost/schedule impact → verification → approval → release → downstream notification/stock disposition.

# Supplier/Fabricator RFQ and Manufacturing Handoff

docs.title: Supplier/Fabricator RFQ and Manufacturing Handoff
docs.text:
Supplier/Fabricator RFQ and Manufacturing Handoff › A good handoff removes ambiguity

Send enough information for the supplier to quote and build the same intent you reviewed. Typical package: RFQ/quantity, drawing PDF, neutral CAD if appropriate, flat DXF for laser parts, BOM, material/finish specification, critical tolerances, weld/assembly notes and revision manifest.

docs.title: Supplier/Fabricator RFQ and Manufacturing Handoff
docs.section: Ask the fabricator for real process data
docs.text:
Supplier/Fabricator RFQ and Manufacturing Handoff › Ask the fabricator for real process data

For repeat work capture their preferred bend radii/tooling, validated bend deductions or bend table, minimum feature preferences, stocked material sizes, hardware installation capability, finish constraints, weld process and inspection capability. Put these in `project-profiles/` so the AI stops guessing.

docs.title: Supplier/Fabricator RFQ and Manufacturing Handoff
docs.text:
Supplier/Fabricator RFQ and Manufacturing Handoff › Quote clarification log

Resolve substitutions, excluded operations, tooling/NRE, minimum order quantities, packaging, test/certification, shipping terms and lead-time assumptions before comparing prices. Cheapest line price is not necessarily the lowest delivered project cost.

docs.title: Supplier/Fabricator RFQ and Manufacturing Handoff
docs.text:
Supplier/Fabricator RFQ and Manufacturing Handoff › Pre-production review

For new or high-risk parts review critical bends, inaccessible fasteners, weld distortion, coating masks, gasket lands, flat-pattern responsibility, revision and inspection points with the supplier before volume production.

# Electrical Enclosure Mechanical Layout and Serviceability

This file covers **mechanical packaging**, not electrical code compliance.

docs.title: Electrical Enclosure Mechanical Layout and Serviceability
docs.text:
Electrical Enclosure Mechanical Layout and Serviceability › Mechanical layout priorities

- Mounting and removal path for every replaceable device.
- Tool access to screws/terminals/filters/fans.
- Cable routing without crushing or impossible bend paths.
- Door swing and equipment interference.
- Heat sources and airflow path.
- Separation of wet/dirty cable-entry zones from sensitive components where relevant.
- Space for labels, grounding/bonding hardware and maintenance.
- Lifting/transport loads and center of gravity.

docs.title: Electrical Enclosure Mechanical Layout and Serviceability
docs.text:
Electrical Enclosure Mechanical Layout and Serviceability › Do not invent electrical clearances

Creepage, clearance, protective bonding, conductor sizing and other electrical safety requirements depend on governing standards, voltage/system conditions and component data. Treat them as supplied/verified requirements from the electrical design authority, not generic AI rules.

docs.title: Electrical Enclosure Mechanical Layout and Serviceability
docs.text:
Electrical Enclosure Mechanical Layout and Serviceability › Serviceability review

Simulate: install, wire, inspect, replace filter/fan, remove mounting plate, open door fully, torque fasteners, clean/drain, and reassemble. A design that works only before wiring is not serviceable.

Engineering Sanity Checks and Calculation Discipline › Overview

# Engineering Sanity Checks and Calculation Discipline

docs.title: Engineering Sanity Checks and Calculation Discipline
docs.text:
Engineering Sanity Checks and Calculation Discipline › Before trusting a result

1. Write units on every input.
2. Label each input SUPPLIED, SOURCE-BACKED, ASSUMED or ESTIMATED.
3. State the model: beam, plate approximation, heat balance, bend model, tolerance stack, cost rollup, etc.
4. Check order of magnitude and limiting cases.
5. Keep more precision internally than you report; do not imply false accuracy.
6. Compare with a second method, known part or prototype when the decision is costly.

docs.title: Engineering Sanity Checks and Calculation Discipline
Engineering Sanity Checks and Calculation Discipline
docs.text:
Engineering Sanity Checks and Calculation Discipline › Output format

For consequential calculations report: formula/model, inputs with provenance, result, sensitivity to uncertain inputs, assumptions, and verification action. If a missing input dominates the result, ask for it instead of manufacturing a precise number.

docs.title: DXF for laser cutting — checks that do not depend on one CAM system
docs.text:
DXF for laser cutting — checks that do not depend on one CAM system › Overview

# DXF for laser cutting — checks that do not depend on one CAM system

DXF is a data exchange format; the **CAM software and machine post-processor decide what is cut, marked or ignored.** What follows are common causes of bad files, not guarantees.

- Units and scale: 1:1, the unit the CAM expects (mm). Wrong units are the most common error.
- One closed contour per cut shape; outer contour plus inner contours (holes). Open or touching-but-not-joined ends fail nesting.
- No duplicate overlapping entities (they cut twice) and no zero-length or tiny stray segments.
- Prefer lines, arcs and circles; splines and ellipses may be converted or rejected by CAM.
- Layers: separate CUT, MARK/ENGRAVE, BEND-LINE, ANNOTATION. Which layer names/colours the CAM maps to which process is a CAM setting; get it from the shop. Do not assume.
- Bend lines and dimension text must not sit on the cut layer.
- Thickness, material, quantity, revision and part number belong in the file name or an accompanying note; do not rely on text inside the DXF.
- Kerf and lead-in/lead-out are normally applied by CAM, not drawn in the DXF, unless the shop says otherwise.
- Always preview the DXF in the CAM (or a viewer) before release: count the contours, check scale with one known dimension.

docs.text:
Metric fasteners — quick reference (verify against the actual standard/product) › Sheet-metal specifics

- Self-clinching studs/nuts/standoffs (PEM-type): required hole size, minimum sheet thickness and edge distance come from the **manufacturer's datasheet** for the exact part number and sheet material. Never infer them.
- Threading directly in thin sheet gives few threads; consider extruded (flow-drilled) holes, clinch nuts or rivet nuts, and say that the choice is a design decision.
- Welded studs (stud welding) mark the opposite face; a drawing must say which face is visible/cosmetic.
- In a laser DXF, a stud/PEM location is either a through hole (cut) or a mark; the file and the CAM mapping must say which.

docs.title: Geometrical tolerancing — symbol groups (ISO 1101 / ASME Y14.5)
docs.text:
Geometrical tolerancing — symbol groups (ISO 1101 / ASME Y14.5) › Overview

# Geometrical tolerancing — symbol groups (ISO 1101 / ASME Y14.5)

Check the current edition. Differences between ISO and ASME practice matter (e.g. fundamental tolerancing principle ISO 8015 vs. ASME Rule #1).

| Group | Characteristic | Needs datum? |
|---|---|---|
| Form | straightness, flatness, circularity, cylindricity | no |
| Profile | profile of a line, profile of a surface | optional (yes if locating) |
| Orientation | perpendicularity, parallelism, angularity | yes |
| Location | position; ISO also concentricity and symmetry | yes |
| Runout | circular runout, total runout | yes (axis datum) |

- ASME Y14.5 (from the 2009 edition) no longer includes concentricity and symmetry; ISO 1101 still does. Confirm which standard the customer drawing uses.
- A tolerance frame reads left to right: symbol | tolerance value (with diameter sign or modifier when needed) | datum references in order of precedence.
- Datums come from functional mounting surfaces, not from whatever is convenient to measure.
- General tolerances: ISO 2768-1 (linear/angular), ISO 2768-2 (geometrical: H, K, L classes); welded constructions: ISO 13920. A general-tolerance note must be on the drawing to apply.

docs.title: Geometrical tolerancing — symbol groups (ISO 1101 / ASME Y14.5)
docs.text:
Geometrical tolerancing — symbol groups (ISO 1101 / ASME Y14.5) › Sheet-metal reminders

- Large thin panels are not flat in free state; a flatness callout needs a stated measurement condition (free/restrained) or use profile of a surface.
- Hole patterns that cross a bend: state which flange carries the datum, and whether the pattern is controlled relative to the same flange.
- Do not tolerance what the process cannot hold; ask the shop for achievable bend and laser tolerances.

docs.section: Sheet-metal design consequences (design intent only — the rating itself comes from testing)
docs.text:
IP Codes (IEC 60529) — quick reference › Sheet-metal design consequences (design intent only — the rating itself comes from testing)

- IP rating is **earned by test**, not by drawing. A design can only *target* a rating.
- IP5x/6x: closed seams, gasketed door, no open through-holes; filter/vent changes the rating.
- IPx4 and above: drip edges / roof slope, door overlap or labyrinth, gasket compression
  defined (groove or flat gasket + stop), cable entries via glands or sealed plates.
- Every cut-out (display, switch, gland, fan) is a seal location; list each one.
- Welded seams that must seal need to be continuous; spot or stitch welds are not a seal by themselves.
- Condensation and drainage are separate from IP; mention them but do not mix them in the rating.
- NEMA / UL enclosure types are **not** one-to-one equivalent to IP codes.

# Evidence labels (use in every technical or commercial answer)

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| SUPPLIED | the user or a document gave this value |
| CALCULATED | derived from other values with the formula shown |
| SOURCE-BACKED | taken from a named source (standard, datasheet, certificate) with edition/date |
| PRACTICE | common engineering/shop practice; shop- or company-dependent |
| ASSUMED | a stated guess made to continue; replace when possible |
| ESTIMATED | an approximate value with an error range |
| UNKNOWN | not available; ask or mark as release blocker |

# Sheet-metal materials — density and handling

Densities below are **nominal textbook values**, rounded. They are a starting point, not a certificate value.
For any mass that goes into a drawing, quotation or shipping document, take density from the
supplier's material certificate / datasheet or from the company material library, and record which one.

| Material (common designation) | Nominal density, kg/m³ (= g/cm³ x 1000) | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Carbon steel (S235/S355, DC01) | ~7850 | |
| Stainless steel 304 / 1.4301 | ~7900-8000 | varies by source |
| Stainless steel 316 / 1.4401 | ~8000 | varies by source |
| Aluminium EN AW-5754 | ~2660-2670 | alloy datasheets differ slightly |
| Aluminium EN AW-5052 | ~2680 | |
| Aluminium EN AW-6061 | ~2700 | |
| Copper (Cu-ETP) | ~8900-8960 | |
| Brass (CuZn37) | ~8400-8500 | |
| Galvanised steel sheet | ~7850 (+ coating) | zinc coating adds a small mass; not in base density |

docs.title: Sheet-metal materials — density and handling
docs.text:
Sheet-metal materials — density and handling › Rules

- Write the alloy, temper and product form (sheet/plate/coil) next to any density you use.
- Nominal thickness is not actual thickness: sheet is supplied within a thickness tolerance; for a mass check, state which one you used.
- Coatings (zinc, powder paint), weld metal, hardware and gaskets are separate mass items.
- A CAD mass equals volume x the density of the material assigned in the model. If the assigned material is wrong or its density was edited, the mass is wrong.
- Mechanical properties (yield, tensile, hardness) depend on temper and standard; never quote them without the standard and temper.

docs.text:
Sheet-metal formulas (check the K-factor source before use) › Overview

# Sheet-metal formulas (check the K-factor source before use)

Symbols: T = thickness, R = inside bend radius, θ = bend angle (angle the flange is turned,
90° for a right-angle bend), K = K-factor (neutral-axis position ÷ T).

- Bend allowance: `BA = θ(rad) × (R + K·T)`   with θ(rad) = θ(°) × π / 180
- Outside setback: `OSSB = (R + T) × tan(θ/2)`
- Bend deduction: `BD = 2 × OSSB − BA`
- Flat length of a part = sum of flat segments + sum of BA (or − sum of BD when dimensions are outside-to-outside)
- Weight: `m = V × ρ`  (keep V in m³ and ρ in kg/m³, or mm³ and kg/mm³; never mix)

K-factor is **not a constant**. It depends on material, thickness, radius, tooling and
method. Use the shop's bend table, the SolidWorks gauge table, or a test bend.
Typical textbook range is 0 < K < 0.5; a number outside the supplier's data is an assumption.

Approximate densities (state the source in any real calculation):
carbon steel ≈ 7850 kg/m³ · stainless 304 ≈ 7900–8000 kg/m³ · aluminium 5052 ≈ 2680 kg/m³.

Terminology Policy (Terim Politikası) › Overview

# Terminology Policy (Terim Politikası)

Terms are chosen in this order. The first rule that applies wins.

1. **SolidWorks interface labels** are copied exactly as the user's installed
   interface shows them. If the label has not been verified, mark it `[doğrulanmadı]`
   and give the English command name instead of guessing a Turkish one.
2. **Standard and drawing terms** follow the standard being cited (ISO / TS EN ISO / ASME).
3. **Established shop-floor terms** are used when the audience is production staff,
   even if a purer Turkish word exists, because the goal is that the person
   reading actually understands.
4. **Öztürkçe (etymologically Turkic) words** are preferred in explanatory text
   whenever they are already in real use and unambiguous
   (e.g. *açınım, büküm, kesim, kaynak, delik*). They are offered as the
   main word in prose, never as a replacement for rules 1 and 2.
5. **Coined words** that nobody in the trade uses are never introduced silently.
   If one is useful, it goes in the glossary as `öneri` next to the established term.

Why this order: a drawing or work order that uses a made-up word gets
mis-read on the shop floor, and a SolidWorks step that names a button that does
not exist wastes the user's time. Language care applies to prose, not to
labels and standards.

AI behavior: when writing Turkish prose, prefer rule-4 words; when quoting UI
or standards, follow rules 1–2; if two words compete, show the established
one first and the Öztürkçe one in parentheses once.

# Engineering Content Maturity Model — v3

Structural type (module/master/blueprint/skill/adapter) and engineering maturity are separate axes.

| Level | Meaning | What it does **not** mean |
|---|---|---|
| `PLANNED` | scope identified | no usable content yet |
| `DRAFT` | initial content exists | not reviewed or tested |
| `IMPLEMENTED` | usable content/tool exists with basic tests/examples | not source- or shop-validated |
| `SOURCE-REVIEWED` | release-relevant external claims traced to current official/supplier sources | not validated against a specific factory/project |
| `DOMAIN-REVIEWED` | reviewed by a competent engineer/domain owner | not proven in production |
| `TESTED` | eval/regression/tool tests pass against defined cases | not production validation |
| `PRODUCTION-VALIDATED` | used/verified on real controlled project/shop data with recorded evidence | not universal certification |

Never write “Complete” merely because a file exists. `PRODUCTION-VALIDATED` is project/process specific and may need to expire after software, tooling, supplier or standard changes.
